---
title: "Figure 3.4: Overall and Trade Policy Uncertainties"
---

![Python: `python/fig-3-4.py`](../images/python/fig-3-4.png)

Monthly uncertainty indices since 2021. World uncertainty (WUI) and trade
policy uncertainty (TPU) are on the left scale; the uncertainty index for
the United States is on the right scale, because its values are much
smaller. Both indices count how often news reports mention uncertainty. A
dotted vertical line marks the start of the Middle East conflict.

**New in this chart:** a right-hand scale with one decimal, and a two-line
label.

## The data

Sheet `data`, 200 rows of monthly data from 2010:

| category | WUI | TPU | USA (right scale) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2010-01-31 | 2.31 | 0.24 | 0.28 |

The dates are at the end of each month (`2010-01-31`). pandas reads them as
dates, not text, because they are stored as dates in the Excel file.

The workbook holds the full history from 2010, but the published chart shows
only January 2021 to August 2026. In Excel this is done by setting the axis
bounds. Here the rows are filtered.

## The script

### Choosing the period

```python
START, END = pd.Timestamp("2021-01-01"), pd.Timestamp("2026-08-31")
CONFLICT = pd.Timestamp("2026-03-01")

data = read_chart_data(STEM)
data = data[(data["category"] >= START) & (data["category"] <= END)]
```

The three dates are set at the top of the script, in capitals, the Python
convention for constants. To update the chart for a new edition, these are
the values to change.

`pd.Timestamp("2021-01-01")` turns the text into a date that can be compared
with the dates in the data. The second line keeps only the rows between
`START` and `END`:

- `data["category"] >= START` gives a column of `True` and `False`, one per
  row.
- `&` combines two such columns: `True` only where both are true. The
  brackets around each comparison are required.
- `data[...]` with a `True`/`False` column keeps the rows where it is
  `True`.

Filtering is not strictly needed, since the x-limits set below would hide
the earlier rows anyway. But it keeps the data small and makes clear what is
plotted. See [Dates on the x-axis](../techniques.qmd#sec-dates).

### The series

```python
left_series = {"WUI": "#00649D", "TPU": "#D55E00"}
usa = "USA (right scale)"
usa_colour = "#666666"
```

The two left-scale series go in a dictionary for the loop. The right-scale
series is kept apart, because it is drawn on a different axes object.

`new_chart()` gets `right=0.4`, much more than the usual 0.15, to leave
room for the right-hand tick labels.

### Two scales

```python
for series, colour in left_series.items():
    ax.plot(data["category"], data[series], color=colour, linewidth=1.7,
            solid_capstyle="round")

# USA is on the right-hand scale.
ax_right = add_right_axis(ax, (0, 3), 0.5)
ax_right.yaxis.set_major_formatter(FormatStrFormatter("%.1f"))
ax_right.tick_params(axis="y", length=2.8)
ax_right.plot(data["category"], data[usa], color=usa_colour, linewidth=1.7,
              solid_capstyle="round")
```

First WUI and TPU are drawn on `ax`. Then `add_right_axis()` creates
`ax_right`, a second plot area on top of the first, with the same x-axis and
its own y-axis on the right. The right-hand scale runs from 0 to 3 in steps
of 0.5. See [A right-hand scale](../chart-style.qmd#sec-right-axis).

The left scale (set below) runs from 0 to 14 in steps of 2: seven intervals.
The right scale has six (3 / 0.5). The ticks on the two sides therefore do
not line up, as in the published chart. Compare
[Figure 5.1](fig-5-1.qmd), where they do.

**One decimal on the right.** `FormatStrFormatter("%.1f")` writes every
label with one decimal: 0.0, 0.5, 1.0, ..., 3.0. `%.1f` is Python's format
code for "a number with one digit after the decimal point", like Excel's
number format `0.0`. Without the formatter, matplotlib would write the
labels as 0.0, 0.5, 1.0, ... as well in this case, but it decides the
format by itself, and the result changes with the scale. Setting it
explicitly matches the published chart whatever the data. See [Number
formats](../techniques.qmd#sec-number-formats).

### The event line and its label

```python
ax.axvline(CONFLICT, color="black", linewidth=0.6, linestyle=(0, (1, 1.5)))
ax.text(CONFLICT - pd.Timedelta(days=15), 1.25, "Middle East\nconflict",
        fontsize=8.7, fontstyle="italic", ha="right", va="bottom",
        linespacing=1.0)
```

`ax.axvline(date)` draws a vertical line across the full height of the plot
at March 2026. The line style `(0, (1, 1.5))` is a custom dash pattern:
start at once (`0`), then repeat a dash 1 line width long and a gap 1.5
line widths long, which gives a fine dotted line. matplotlib measures dash
patterns in line widths, so the pattern scales if the line gets thicker. See [Line
styles](../techniques.qmd#sec-line-styles).

The label is placed with `ax.text(x, y, text)`, in data coordinates:

- **x** is 15 days before the line. `pd.Timedelta(days=15)` is a duration
  that can be subtracted from a date.
- **y** is 1.25 on the left scale, near the bottom of the plot, where the
  lines leave room.
- `ha="right"` aligns the right edge of the text with x, so the label ends
  just before the line. `va="bottom"` puts the bottom of the text at y.
- The label has a line break (`\n`), so it fits in the space before the
  dotted line. `linespacing=1.0` keeps the two lines close together.

The text is written on `ax`, so its y-position is on the left scale. See
[Text, arrows and coordinates](../techniques.qmd#sec-text).

### The axes

```python
ax.set_xlim(START, END)
ax.set_xticks(pd.date_range(START, "2026-07-01", freq="6MS"))
ax.xaxis.set_major_formatter(mdates.DateFormatter("%b-%y"))
ax.tick_params(axis="x", labelrotation=90, length=2.8)

set_y_scale(ax, 0, 14, 2)
ax.tick_params(axis="y", length=2.8)
```

- **The x-limits** are the same dates used to filter the rows.
- **The ticks.** `pd.date_range(START, "2026-07-01", freq="6MS")` gives the
  first day of every sixth month: Jan-21, Jul-21, Jan-22, ..., Jul-26.
- **The labels** are formatted as `Jan-21` with `DateFormatter("%b-%y")`
  and written vertically.
- **The left scale** runs from 0 to 14 with a tick every 2.

### The legend

```python
styles = {**left_series, usa: usa_colour}
ax_right.legend(
    [Line2D([], [], color=c, linewidth=1.8) for c in styles.values()],
    list(styles),
    loc="upper left", bbox_to_anchor=(0.03, 1.0), handlelength=3.0,
    labelspacing=0.1,
)
```

The lines are on two axes objects, so neither knows all three. The legend
is therefore built from sample lines (`Line2D`), one per colour, with the
names from `styles`. It is placed on `ax_right`, the top layer, so no line
is drawn over it. See [A right-hand scale](../techniques.qmd#sec-right-scale)
and [Legends](../techniques.qmd#sec-legends).

## Changing the chart

- **A longer period.** Change `END` and the last tick date. If the labels
  get crowded, use `freq="12MS"` for one label a year.
- **A different event.** Change `CONFLICT` and the label text. If the line
  is close to the left edge, put the label to the right of it: add 15 days
  instead of subtracting, and use `ha="left"`.
- **Aligned ticks.** For ticks that line up on both sides, give the right
  scale seven intervals too, for example `add_right_axis(ax, (0, 3.5), 0.5)`.

## The complete script

The full `python/fig-3-4.py`, as it runs:

```` {.python filename="python/fig-3-4.py"}
"""Figure 3.4: Overall and Trade Policy Uncertainties."""
import matplotlib.dates as mdates
import pandas as pd
from matplotlib.lines import Line2D
from matplotlib.ticker import FormatStrFormatter

from chart_style import (
    add_right_axis,
    new_chart,
    read_chart_data,
    save_chart,
    set_y_scale,
)

STEM = "fig-3-4"

START, END = pd.Timestamp("2021-01-01"), pd.Timestamp("2026-08-31")
CONFLICT = pd.Timestamp("2026-03-01")

data = read_chart_data(STEM)
data = data[(data["category"] >= START) & (data["category"] <= END)]

left_series = {"WUI": "#00649D", "TPU": "#D55E00"}
usa = "USA (right scale)"
usa_colour = "#666666"

fig, ax = new_chart(
    title="Overall and Trade Policy Uncertainties",
    subtitle="(Index)",
    caption=(
        "Sources: Ahir, H, N Bloom, and D Furceri (2022), “World Uncertainty\n"
        "Index”, NBER Working Paper; Caldara and others (2020); and Haver\n"
        "Analytics.\n"
        "Note: The uncertainty measures are news- and media-outlets-based\n"
        "indices that quantify media attention to global news related to overall\n"
        "uncertainty (WUI) and trade policy uncertainty (TPU). Uncertainty index\n"
        "shown for the United States is from the WUI."
    ),
    left=0.3,
    right=0.4,
    bottom_gap=0.5,
)

for series, colour in left_series.items():
    ax.plot(data["category"], data[series], color=colour, linewidth=1.7,
            solid_capstyle="round")

# USA is on the right-hand scale.
ax_right = add_right_axis(ax, (0, 3), 0.5)
ax_right.yaxis.set_major_formatter(FormatStrFormatter("%.1f"))
ax_right.tick_params(axis="y", length=2.8)
ax_right.plot(data["category"], data[usa], color=usa_colour, linewidth=1.7,
              solid_capstyle="round")

ax.axvline(CONFLICT, color="black", linewidth=0.6, linestyle=(0, (1, 1.5)))
ax.text(CONFLICT - pd.Timedelta(days=15), 1.25, "Middle East\nconflict",
        fontsize=8.7, fontstyle="italic", ha="right", va="bottom",
        linespacing=1.0)

ax.set_xlim(START, END)
ax.set_xticks(pd.date_range(START, "2026-07-01", freq="6MS"))
ax.xaxis.set_major_formatter(mdates.DateFormatter("%b-%y"))
ax.tick_params(axis="x", labelrotation=90, length=2.8)

set_y_scale(ax, 0, 14, 2)
ax.tick_params(axis="y", length=2.8)

styles = {**left_series, usa: usa_colour}
ax_right.legend(
    [Line2D([], [], color=c, linewidth=1.8) for c in styles.values()],
    list(styles),
    loc="upper left", bbox_to_anchor=(0.03, 1.0), handlelength=3.0,
    labelspacing=0.1,
)

save_chart(fig, STEM)
````
